[Grifﬁths et al., 2005, Wallach, 2006, Wang et al., 2007] into hierarchical latent topics. In this

model, each sentence is viewed as hierarchical topics with respect to contextual information.

Contextual information is also represented as a probabilistic distribution by training a large data

corpus before summarising documents to ensure the summarisation systems are contextually

embedded. Conversely, though CTM avoids using human summaries to train models, it still

requires training under a larger dataset, which sometimes causes performance issues. Indeed,

another limitation of this model is its poor capability to capture word co-occurrence among

multiple words.

The success of Bayesian topic models has inspired this study to develop a novel model that

uses only their advantages to further enhance MDS performance. However, this research must

also apply special attention to address the aforementioned problems presented in former works.

### 2.3.2 Indicator Representation Approaches

Indicator representation approaches use a list of indicators of importance (such as sentence

length and position, and the presence of speciﬁc phrases; however, any of the aforementioned

topic representation methods can serve as the basis of indicators) to represent sentences in text

sources. Indicator representation approaches generate such representations of documents, then

directly use an indicator list to rank sentences by importance. While graph methods employ

a single importance indicator derived from the centrality of sentences, other approaches may

heuristically combine a set of different importance indicators using machine learning algorithms

to determine which sentences should be included in a summary.

### 2.3.2.1 Graph Models

Recently, graph models have been widely used as a typical method of indicator representation

in automatic text summarisation [Canhasi and Kononenko, 2014, Ferreira et al., 2014, Glavaˇs

### 2.3.2.2 Machine Learning Approaches

Unlike graph models, which typically base summarisation on a single indicator, machine learn-

ing approaches employ a variety of indicators of importance learnt from input data. This

approach combines these indicators to generate weighted feature vectors to represent sentences

and topics, which then uses machine learning to decide which sentences to select to form a

summary.

Machine learning approaches can be supervised, unsupervised or semi-supervised. Learning

from a training set of documents and their respective human-produced summaries, a supervised

approach treats summary extraction as a binary classiﬁcation problem, which classiﬁes indi-

vidual sentences in input documents in either summary or non-summary classes. Some of the

classiﬁers based on supervised learning algorithms - such as mathematical regression (MR)

[Fattah and Ren, 2009], Naive Bayes classiﬁer [Fattah, 2014], Support Vector machine (SVM)

[Fattah, 2014, Wan and Zhang, 2014], and Neural Networks [Cao et al., 2015a,b, Fattah and

Ren, 2009, Zhang et al., 2017] can be utilised in supervised machine learning approaches to

learn useful features of sentences and to select summary sentences. In contrast, unsupervised

machine learning methods do not require training data or human-generated summaries. In-

stead, they employ unsupervised learning techniques - such as Hidden Markov Model (HMM)

[Conroy and O’leary, 2001], clustering [Yang et al., 2014] - to discover hidden structures in


<!-- Page 51 -->

documents’ most important sentences to create summaries.

### 2.3.3 Sentences Selection in Extractive MDS

In extractive MDS, summary sentences are selected from input documents. An extractive

summariser selects the best combination of important sentences to form a length-limited short

summary. Based on the different intermediate representations adapted, the importance of sen-

tences can be identiﬁed and measured accordingly. However, given some constraints imposed

on a summary - such as maximising its informative nature or content relevance, minimising

repetition and conforming to a required summary length [Nenkova and McKeown, 2012] - and

a set of important sentences deriving from different documents, the task of selecting the best

combination of sentences to form a summary becomes a non-deterministic polynomial-time

hardness (NP-hard) problem [Filatova and Hatzivassiloglou, 2004]. There are two possible

methods to solve this problem in MDS: adopt a greedy algorithm extracting a summary sentence

by sentence or optimise a summary directly by exploiting global optimisation algorithms.

### 2.3.3.1 Greedy Approaches

If formalising the sentence selection for MDS as a Maximal Set Coverage problem, a greedy

algorithm has been proven to be the best polynomial approximation [Hochbaum, 1997] for

an NP-hard problem. Generally, greedy algorithms for sentence selection in MDS have the

following components [Dunne, 2006]:

• A candidate sentence set from which a summary is created that can be either whole

sentence collections or identiﬁed top-n most important sentences.

• A set of candidates that have already been ‘used’.

• A selection function, which chooses the best candidate sentence to be added to a summary.


<!-- Page 54 -->


2.3. EXTRACTIVE DOCUMENT SUMMARISATION 27

• A feasibility function, which determines if a candidate sentence can be added to a sum-

mary

• An objective function, which assigns a value to a summary, or a partial summary.

• A completion indicator, which indicates when the complete summary is discovered.

A widely adopted greedy approach for both generic and query-focused MDS is Maximal Marginal

Relevance (MMR) [Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998, Lin et al., 2010, Xie and Liu, 2008, Yan and

Wan, 2014]. The MMR method ﬁrst adds the most informative sentence (i.e., the most relevant

to a user’s query for query-focused MDS or has highest importance score in generic MDS)

to a summary. At each selection step, the selection function together with the feasibility and

objective function in the greedy algorithm are constrained to select sentences one by one, of

which their similarity with already selected sentences is minimal (to control redundancy) and

the informative nature of the intended summary at its given stage is maximal.

### 2.3.3.2 Global Optimisation Methods

Unlike greedy approaches that incrementally include sentences that maximise the selection

criteria, global-optimisation algorithms attempt to directly ﬁnd the best sentence combinations

across all input sentences by using global inference algorithms. Dynamic programming and

integer linear programming (ILP) are two major global inference algorithms adopted in MDS.

While a dynamic programming algorithm can be used to ﬁnd approximate solutions for an

NP-hard problem [McDonald, 2007, Wang et al., 2017, Ye et al., 2007], ILP can provide an

exact solution for an optimisation problem during the sentence selection process [Alguliev et

al., 2013, McDonald, 2007, Woodsend and Lapata, 2012]. Dynamic programming algorithms

simplify the global inference for summary selection by breaking it down into simpler sub-

problems (e.g., a sequence of decision steps over time) in a recursive manner; thus, the best

combination can be found quickly using various search techniques. However, the performance

of approximate dynamic programming algorithms is lower than the exact solutions provided by

ILP approaches. Modern ILP solvers are well studied to solve moderately large optimisation

problems with efﬁcient branch and bound algorithms [McDonald, 2007]. However, as the

running time for an ILP algorithm increases quadratically with the size of input, its scalability

and, therefore, feasibility, is limited.

selection in extractive MDS, it must optimise three compulsory requirements: be informative

and relevant, contain least redundancy and feature a constrained summary length.

### 2.4 Pattern Mining Models in Document Summarisation

While automatic document summarisation suffers from inaccuracies, frequent sequential pat-

tern mining (which aims to discover patterns carrying more semantic meanings) is still con-

sidered open and exploratory in the ﬁeld. Pattern mining has been widely employed to solve

problems in data mining, web intelligence and IR communities for years. Compared to term-

based methods, multi-word patterns capitalising on phrases are more discriminative and carry

more semantics [Xu and Li, 2007, Yan et al., 2005]. Some mature techniques such as maximal

patterns, closed patterns and master patterns have been developed as effective alternatives to

phrases with reduced redundancy and ‘noisy’ patterns [Wu et al., 2004]. Li et al. [2010]

proposed a pattern-mining approach for discovery relevance features in IR systems, which

integrate both term and pattern features by deploying higher level features (patterns) over low-

level features (terms) [Li et al., 2015]. Gao et al. [2013b] combined pattern-mining techniques

with LDA topic modelling to generate more discriminative and semantically rich topic repre-

sentations using patterns rather than single words [Gao et al., 2015].

Conversely, there are few successful attempts [Baralis et al., 2012, 2013, Qiang et al., 2016]

to adapt well-established pattern mining techniques for automatic document summarisation,

as two fundamental problems limit their feasibility in document summarisation [Zhong et al.,

2012]. The ﬁrst regards a low frequency of speciﬁc patterns along with highly frequent general

patterns, thus, impeding pattern discovery from achieving the best balance between specialisa-

tion and generalisation in a document’s topic representation. The second regards how best to

interpret discovered patterns to accurately measure the importance of sentences in extractive

document summarisation. Therefore, to develop an effective pattern-based approach, the low

frequency of speciﬁc patterns and the misinterpretation of discovered patterns must be properly

addressed.

### 2.4.1 Attempts to Exploit FPs in MDS

An itemset-based summariser (ItemSum) [Baralis et al., 2012] is one of the nearest work ex-

ploiting FPs in document summarisation. Besides traditional BOW document representations,

ItemSum employs a transactional representation of a documents set to extract its FPs and

generate a pattern-based model. With respect to such pattern-based models and considering

both sentence model coverage and sentence relevance scores using TF-IDF statistics, the most

representative and non-redundant sentences are selected to be included in a summary. Baralis et

al. [2012] claimed ItemSum is the ﬁrst attempt at using a pattern-based approach in document

summarisation. Later, they exploited FP mining to discover association rules to represent the

correlations among multiple terms in a general purpose graph-based summariser [Baralis et

al., 2013], namely GraphSum. In GraphSum, a lift [Tan et al., 2002] measure is used to

evaluate positive and negative correlations among the extracted association rules between a

pair of terms. GraphSum adopts a variant from a traditional PageRank [Brin and Page, 2012]

graph-ranking strategy to discriminate between positive and negative term correlations; this

helps select the most informative sentences both with the best coverage and a high relevance

score in a correlation graph to form summaries. However, the FPs exploited in both ItemSum

and GraphSum have a limited disambiguation of topic representations (i.e., the FPs are often

not discriminative enough to represent speciﬁc topics). Further, too many redundant patterns in

FPs impair the performance of a summariser.

Unlike ItemSum’s exploitation of FPs, Qiang et al. [2016] proposed PatSum, a method

employing frequent closed patterns (FCPs) for generic MDS. To consider the semantic infor-

mation of a document’s content and avoid the labour involved (as well as a lack of requirement

for additional semantic resources), PatSum addressed the drawbacks of term-based methods

by exploiting closed patterns to represent all sentences. Figure 2.7 illustrates the pattern-based

representation it used, demonstrating how it differs from traditional term-based methods. Pat-

Sum calculated sentence rankings and sentence similarities through discovered closed patterns,

which belong to sentences. Though PatSum improved the performance of pattern-based models

by removing redundant patterns, it still ignored the issue of topical coherence in multi-document

summaries. Nonetheless, knowing how to adapt closed patterns for an effective measure of both

query relevance and topic coverage in query-focused MDS is still an open problem.

### 2.4.2 Pattern-based Topic Models

PBTMs [Gao et al., 2013a] were originally proposed for information ﬁltering (IF). They inte-

grate statistic topic modelling techniques with data mining techniques to generate discriminative

and semantically rich representations for topics and documents. Pattern-based representations

can represent both more meaningfully and more accurately than word-based representations,

and, as they contain structural information, the associations between multiple words can be

easily revealed.

In PBTMs, two steps are proposed to discover semantically meaningful and efﬁcient pat-

terns to represent topics and documents. The ﬁrst constructs a new transactional dataset from the

LDA [Blei et al., 2003] outcomes of a document collection, and the second uses transactional

datasets to generate pattern-enhanced topic representations to model a user’s interests across

multiple topics. PBTMs use both frequent and closed patterns not only to represent topics, but

also to represent topic relevance - indeed, using topic distribution to represent a collection of

documents and, likewise, semantic patterns to represent topics, is innovative. Unlike other

pattern mining models, which generate patterns from a collection of documents, a PBTM

generates patterns from the topic representations produced by an LDA model. As such, one

topic generates one transactional dataset from which the discovered patterns are more sensitive

to affecting accurate representations of a given topic. Moreover, it is proven that PBTMs can

generate longer patterns than other pattern-mining models, such as frequent sequence closed


<!-- Page 58 -->


2.5. DOCUMENT SUMMARISATION EVALUATION 31

patterns or single words in LDA. Therefore, PBTM patterns are more speciﬁc and meaningful

than either two models.

Though PBTMs demonstrated superior performance compared to many state-of-the-art term-

based models for IF and IR applications, Gao et al. [2015] proposed the maximum matched

pattern-based topic model (MPBTM), another enhanced PBTM to further improve the repre-

sentation of users’ information needs. Its most innovative feature (as compared with original

PBTMs) is its ability to organise discovered topical patterns into groups (called equivalence

classes) in terms of their taxonomic and statistical features. The patterns in each group have

the same frequency and represent similar semantic meaning to identify the most representative

patterns; this helps estimate a document’s relevance in relation to users’ information needs more

effectively.

As reviewed in Section 2.3.1, topic representation approaches have been proven as suc-

cessful methods in document summarisation. Considering a PBTM may have the potential to

construct proper topic representations of text documents, one can assume that exploiting them

in document summarisation would outperform purely term-based approaches. Conversely, both

PBTMs and MPBTMs require supervised training to obtain a relevance model, thus, introducing

the issue of how best to adapt PBTMs in an unsupervised manner to achieve success for MDS

tasks; this concerns both generic and query-focused summarisation.

### 2.5 Document Summarisation Evaluation

### 2.5.1 Challenge

Evaluating automatic document summarisation is a difﬁcult task, and manual evaluation is an

expensive feat, as it necessitates humans to read not only summaries but also multiple source

documents. Evidently, such human judgements on what can be considered ‘good’ or satisfactory

summaries are an ambiguous task, thus, making evaluation particularly challenging.

Similar to NLP systems, summarisation systems can be assessed either by intrinsic or extrin-

sic evaluation [Jones and Galliers, 1996]. An intrinsic evaluation directly analyses a summary

to determine its quality on the basis of the coverage or overlap between a machine-made

and human-made summary [Gambhir and Gupta, 2017]. Conversely, an extrinsic evaluation


<!-- Page 59 -->


32 CHAPTER 2. LITERATURE REVIEW

determines the quality of a summarisation based on how it affects the performance of other

tasks such as text classiﬁcation, IR and question answering. The coherence and informative

nature of a summary is usually assessed by the former method, whereas the latter examines

both relevance and reading comprehension .

In practice, the most common method to evaluate an automatic MDS is to compare system-

generated summaries with human-generated summaries. Indeed, the document summarisation

community has sought a standard human or automatic evaluation metric to help compare dif-

ferent summariser systems or establish a baseline. Essentially, these should produce reliable

scores that bear high correlations with human judgements [Hovy et al., 2006].

### 2.5.2 ROUGE

Lin [2004] introduced ROUGE 1: Recall-Oriented Understudy of Gisting Evaluation, a set of

metrics and a software package used for automated evaluation of summaries. ROUGE was

inspired by BLEU (bilingual evaluation understudy) [Papineni et al., 2002], which automati-

cally evaluates machine translation system’s quality of text output. Similar to BLEU, ROUGE

relies on n-gram (a contiguous sequence of n words) co-occurrences statistics between summary

pairs. According to different n and different strategies, multiple ROUGE metrics are deﬁned as

follows [Lin, 2004]:

1. ROUGE-N: regards n-gram recall based co-occurrence statistics, including unigrams (ROUGE-

1) and bigrams (ROUGE-2). It compares the n-gram of two summaries, and counts the

number of matches. ROUGE-N is computed as follows:

### 2.6 Chapter Summary

Automatic document summarisation addresses the problem of information overload. Indeed,

numerous approaches have been proposed to meet the challenge of creating satisfactory sum-

maries for processing large scale text documents; however, this review has concentrated on

extractive summarisation approaches. As shown, there are three relatively independent tasks in

an extractive summarisation process: creating the intermediate representation of a text source,

measuring sentences’ importance and selecting summary sentences [Nenkova and McKeown,

2012]. Indeed, multiple variations of an extractive approach have been proposed across the

latter half of the twentieth century. Two different types of approaches - topic representation

approaches and indicator representation approaches - have been contrasted in terms of how

they represent a document source. Along with these approaches come the Bayesian topic model

and graph-based models, which have recently gained wider popularity and particular emphasis

within this review. Topic representation approaches have employed various topic modelling

methods to model the content of source documents (including many popular summarisation

methods), whereas indicator representation approaches combining some new machine learning

algorithms have proven effective in MDS. However, most of the aforementioned approaches

possess a general weakness to capture the hidden semantic meanings and correlations among

text sources, thus, resulting in coherence and cohesion issues - two particularly challenging


<!-- Page 62 -->


2.6. CHAPTER SUMMARY 35

issues in extractive document summarisation. Though the latest technology in deep learning and

AI can be used to solve such problems in MDS, their complexity and difﬁculty to implement

both limits their feasibility. Therefore, well-established pattern mining techniques aiming to

discover hidden semantic meanings and correlations among text data could be exploited as an

alternative to word-embedding approaches and beneﬁt extractive document summarisation.

Pattern mining techniques combined with statistical topic modelling (which emphasises

the strength of IR) have yet to be explored in depth within document summarisation ﬁelds.

However, this proposed research has attempted to exploit PBTMs [Gao et al., 2013a, 2015]

- which can automatically generate discriminative and semantically rich representations for

modelling topics and documents as a novel topic representation approach - to improve the

accuracy of document summarisation. To meet the speciﬁc requirements of a query-focused

multi-document summariser, this study also developed an effective pattern-enhanced query

relevance model combining query expansion techniques with three-way decision rules to further

enhance the representing power of query relevant patterns. While this research attempted to

ease limitations on the low frequency of speciﬁc patterns and the misinterpretation of patterns

discovered in pattern-based approaches, issues in extractive document summarisation (such

as redundancy, temporal dimension, coreference or sentence ordering [Lloret and Palomar,

2012] should also be considered. Thus, this study used ROUGE, a standard metric for the

automatic evaluation of document summarisation (as described in Section 2.5.2), to evaluate

the performance of the proposed summarisation systems.

## Pattern-enhanced Topic Models for MDS

PBTMs were originally proposed for IF [Gao et al., 2013a, 2015]. In this chapter, a generic

multi-document summariser is proposed to exploit PBTMs to automatically generate discrimi-

native and semantically rich representations for MDS, without the use of semantic resources or

training data. The proposed model (namely PETMSum) combines pattern-mining techniques

with LDA topic modelling to capture not only the contextual information of words and sentences

but also their hidden correlations. This information has previously been published in two

conference papers [Wu et al., 2015, 2016].

As an extractive multi-document summariser, PETMSum performs three tasks: creating an

intermediate representation, and scoring and selecting sentences. This study attempts to adapt

PBTMs for use in extractive MDS to represent each sentence in documents and increase its

suitability for extractive summary; typically, these should be composed of the most representa-

tive and non-redundant sentences to capture only documents’ major topics. However, the main

purpose of using LDA topic modelling in MDS is to capture common topic structures among

documents in a given collection, thus, allowing a generated summary to reserve similar topic

structures as input documents. Therefore, in PETMSum, even pattern mining is based on a

sentence level, topic modelling should be maintained on both a document and collection level.

Essentially, PETMSum ﬁrst generates pattern-enhanced topic representations for sentences

and document sets. Then, with respect to the discovered correlations and semantic meanings

carried by sentences’ topical patterns, PETMSum scores the saliency of sentences based on their

pattern-enhanced topic representation; next, it selects the most important sentences based on

maximum coverage and least redundancy to form a ﬁnal summary. The architecture of the

### 3.1 Preliminaries

### 3.1.1 LDA Topic Modelling

LDA [Blei et al., 2003] - the most common topic model currently in use - is a generative

statistical topic modelling technique for discovering the hidden topics that occur in a collection

of documents. In LDA, every document is considered a probabilistic mixture of various topics.

Each topic is then considered in relation to the probability distribution of terms that appear in

said documents. In a document collection D consisting of M documents, for the ith word in

a document d, denoted as wd,i, the LDA model speciﬁes the distribution over words within a

Based on whether a word’s occurrence is considered as related to a topic, LDA can assign

a set of words to a speciﬁc topic. Thus, this study will use these assignments to establish

topic-sentence transactional tables, which form the input for pattern discovery in constructing

pattern-enhanced topic representations.

### 3.1.2 Pattern Mining

This study assumes all documents are split into sentences. Thus, a given multi-document

collection D yields a set of sentences. For pattern mining, sentences rather than documents

are used as transaction rows and a set of terms are transaction columns to form transactional

tables Γ, where succinct informative term-sets - which appear frequently in sentences with a

frequency no less than a user speciﬁed minimal support threshold σ - can be discovered.

Deﬁnition 1. (support): the support of a pattern X, denoted as supp(X), is the percentage


<!-- Page 67 -->


40 CHAPTER 3. PATTERN-ENHANCED TOPIC MODELS FOR MDS

of transactions in a given transactional table Γ, which contains X.

Deﬁnition 2. (frequent pattern): a pattern X is termed frequent pattern if its support

supp(X) >= σ, a given minimal support.

Deﬁnition 3. (closed pattern): for a transactional table, a pattern X is a closed pattern if

there is not a single pattern X′, such that (1) X ⊂X′, and (2) supp(X) = supp(X′).

Essentially, a closed pattern can reveal the relations of the largest range of associated terms,

as it covers all information described in its subsets.

The proposed model in this study adopts closed pattern for multiple reasons: the number of

closed patterns is signiﬁcantly smaller than the number of FPs for a dataset, and closed patterns

are considered more effective and efﬁcient to represent sentences than FPs due to their attractive

features [Gao et al., 2015, Wu et al., 2015, Xu et al., 2011, Zaki and Hsiao, 2002].

### 3.4 Sentence Selection

In generic MDS tasks, sentence selection should be based on maximal information coverage

and least redundancy, but in extraction-based MDS the most important sentences derive from

multiple similar documents, thus, amplifying the importance of redundancy control. MMR

[Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998] and clustering [Radev et al., 2004] are two major approaches

that can be widely adopted to avoid redundancy in MDS systems. In MMR, sentences are

added to summaries one by one; at every selection step, these must possess both the highest

importance score among the unselected candidate sentences and minimal information redun-

dancy with the sentences already present in the generated summary. Conversely, in clustering-

based approaches, input sentences are clustered to multiple clusters before being selected to

a summary; this ensures redundancy control can be achieved by selecting only one or a few

sentences from each cluster to form ﬁnal summaries.


<!-- Page 74 -->


3.4. SENTENCE SELECTION 47

The proposed PETMSum applies an effective method to select sentences for generic sum-

marisation, combining clustering with an MMR greedy approach, which is similar to a ranking-

based clustering model [Yang et al., 2014] but applies a diversity-penalty imposition [Wan,

2008, Yan and Wan, 2014] to reduce redundancy further. First, for each identiﬁed important

topic, one set of top-n ranking sentences were derived using Equation 3.3. The ﬁrst sentence

in the ﬁnal summary had the highest score from the most important topic cluster (i.e., the topic

weight score generated by LDA topic modelling is largest). Upon ranking the topic clusters

in descending order by weight, sentences with the highest diversity-penalty-imposed score

among the remaining sentences were added one by one using the following equation, which

was formulated in SRRank [Yan and Wan, 2014].

Score(t+1) (si) = Score(t) (si) −δ × CosSim (si, sl) × ScoreSR (sl) , (3.6)

where sl is the last selected sentence from the current topic cluster with the highest ranking

score, si is the remaining sentence which is going to be penalized, and CosSim (si, sl) is the

normalised cosine similarity between the two sentences si and sl. The penalty weight parameter

δ was set to 0.7 since this value produced the best results for the PETMSum model. The

selection and penalisation were completed in an iterative manner until the summary length

reached its limit. In addition, to integrate the sentence lengths along with the selection process,

extra selection criteria were established to maintain the same ranking score for one topic, retain

the shortest score and discard the others, as it can be assumed that if more than one sentence for

topic Zj has the same score of topic signiﬁcance Tsig (Zj, s) (by Equation 3.2), the shortest is

the best to represent that level of sentence importance. By applying these criteria, the derived

set of top-n ranking sentences is the best of best sentence candidates for one speciﬁc topic.

It includes the process of selecting the shortest sentences with equal topic signiﬁcance scores to

### 3.5 Pattern-enhanced Topic Models for Query-focused MDS

Query-focused MDSs must to generate summaries that not only cover the most important

content in a document, but also contain relevant answers to users’ given queries. Essentially,

the proposed pattern-enhanced topic model can be adopted to meet the special requirements

of query-focused MDS tasks, ﬁrst by using topical patterns to measure the query relevance

between a query and a speciﬁc topic, and then by selecting the most relevant topics to be covered

in the summary. Ideally, this process produces summaries that both bias users’ queries and cover

documents’ most important topics.

### 3.5.1 Measuring Query Relevance of Topics

Similar to gauging topic signiﬁcance, query relevance can be measured by exploiting the sig-

niﬁcance of matched topical relevant patterns in a given query. Considering queries usually

contain few terms, each should be considered as an important factor determining its relevance.

Therefore, when applying topic signiﬁcance, topical pattern matching can be slightly suspended

by permitting partial matches containing at least one query term. However, it is important that

partial and full matches should be treated with different weights.

### 3.5.2 Selecting Query Relevant Topics

In query-focused MDS, the topic selection should consider both importance and query rele-

vance. Thus, before using Algorithm 1 to select topics, each topic is assigned a different weight

for generic MDS. However, in PETMSum, these weights concern just the topic distribution (wj

) set by LDA. Conversely, for a query-focused MDS, the topic weight of topic Zj is calculated

using the following equation:

W (Zj) = (1 −λ) × wj + λ × Tsig (Zj, q) , (3.9)

where λ is a constant value to indicate the weight coefﬁcient of a topic’s query relevance. In

this study, it was set to 0.5 as default and could be tuned for slightly better performance as well.

Therefore, the weight of each topic is assigned based on both its topic distribution and query

relevance, and the top ranked topics are not only statistically important but also biased to user

directed queries. In covering the selected topics, PETMSum can generate summaries meeting

the special requirements of query-focused MDS.

### 3.6 Experiment and Evaluation Methodology

In this section, two sets of experiments for a generic MDS task were conducted to verify two

hypotheses:

• Hypothesis 1: The proposed pattern-enhanced topic representation is more effective

than other topic representations in a Bayesian topic model based summariser.

• Hypothesis 2: The proposed pattern-enhanced topic model is an effective unsupervised

approach for generic MDS tasks.

An extensive experimental campaign was also conducted to address:

• An analysis of how topic selection affects a pattern-enhanced topic representation (see

section 3.2)

• A performance comparison between the proposed PETMSum using topical clustering-

based MMR sentence selection, with one variant based on joint ranking MMR and several

### 3.6.1 Dataset

The proposed generic MDS method was evaluated using a Document Understanding Confer-

ence 3 (DUC) 2004 dataset, which is an English-written open-benchmark dataset for automatic

summarisation evaluation. DUC 2004 involved 50 document clusters, every one of which

consists of approximately 10 news articles, with an average of 280 sentences for each cluster.

Essentially, the task was to create a summary of no more than 665 bytes for each document set,

for which DUC 2004 provided at least one ‘golden’ summaries written by domain experts and

eight manual summaries authored by human assessors for evaluation.

In the experiments, each document in the DUC 2004 dataset was segmented into sentences,

with their stop words removed to construct transactional tables for pattern mining. Snowball’s

Porter2 stemming algorithm [Porter et al., 2002] was then used for word stemming.

On DUC 2004 dataset, extensive experiments were conducted using different topic repre-

sentations to verify the ﬁrst hypothesis; the resulting dataset was then applied to formally assess

the integrated system of the proposed generic MDS approach.

### 3.6.2 Evaluation Metric

The ROUGE toolkit [Lin, 2004] was used to evaluate the performance of this study’s summari-

sation systems. Indeed, the DUC also adopted this kit as their ofﬁcial evaluation metric for

automatic document summarisation because its metrics automatically determine the quality of

a summary by counting the number of overlapping units, such as n-grams, word sequences and

the word pairs between either a candidate summary and an ‘ideal’ summary or a set of ‘ideal’

summaries created by humans.

### 3.6.3 Baselines

### 3.6.3.1 For Verifying First Hypothesis

Pattern-enhanced topic representation is a novel part of PETMSum. To validate its signif-

icance in a Bayesian topic model for MDS, the following baseline methods were deﬁned,

employing different topic representations to allow for comparisons with this study’s pattern-

enhanced topic representation MDS system. Essentially, these methods were created on the

same LDA topic-model-based summarisation system using different score factors to calculate

sentences’ topic signiﬁcance based on different topic representations:

• WTWSum: uses LDA word-topic weights for scoring sentences. LDA word-topic weight

can be acquired from LDA results based on word-topic assignment and word-topic distri-

bution.

• FPSum: uses FPs to represent topic and sentence. FPs are generated from pattern

discovery phrase using the same topic-sentence transactional table introduced in Section

3.2

### 3.6.3.2 For Verifying Second Hypothesis

In the formal evaluation experiment, the proposed PETMSum method was compared with both

the DUC 2004 participating systems and the following most widely used or recently published

methods for generic MDS as its baseline systems:

• Centroid [Radev et al., 2004]: extracts sentences based on three major sentence features:

the distance to centroid value, the ﬁrst sentence overlap and positional value.

3.7. EVALUATION RESULTS 53

• LexPageRank [Erkan and Radev, 2004b]: is a graph method that selects the most signiﬁ-

cant sentences by calculating their lexical eigenvector centrality in a sentence connectivity

graph based on sentence-to-sentence cosine similarity.

• LSA [Gong and Liu, 2001]: is a method using latent semantic analysis on terms to

extract ‘semantically’ important sentences with the greatest combined weights across all

important topics.

• BSTM [Wang et al., 2009]: is a Bayesian sentence-based topic model using both term-

document and term-sentence associations.

• DSR-G [Wei et al., 2010]: is an unsupervised document-sensitive graph model that ex-

ploits document-document and document-sentence relations to distinguish intra-document

sentence relations from inter-document sentence relations; it also considers the inﬂuence

of an entire document set on individual sentence evaluations.

• ItemSum [Baralis et al., 2012]: is the ﬁrst attempt at exploiting FPs for MDS by selecting

sentences based on compact subset of frequent itemsets.

• GraphSum [Baralis et al., 2013]: is a graph-based summariser that employs association

rules to represent correlations among multiple terms; it then adopts a graph ranking

strategy to discriminate between positive and negative term correlations for sentence

selection.

• wHAASum [Canhasi and Kononenko, 2016]: is based on wAA analysis; this method

selects ‘the best of the best’ summary sentences.

### 3.7.5 Impact of Minimal Support Threshold

For pattern mining, the user speciﬁed minimal support threshold σ (see Section 3.1.2 and 3.2)

is an important parameter that could inﬂuence the performance of pattern-based methods. To

analyse its impact on PETMSum, a set of experiments varying the value of σ in the range of 2%

and 7% were conducted. Figure 3.2 shows the results of PETMSum upon varying the value of

minimal support σ in a topical pattern discovery step.

As demonstrated, when increasing the value of σ, performance increases initially but de-

clines thereafter. The best performance was achieved when σ = 3.5% for both ROUGE-2

and ROUGE-SU4. Subsequently, the results dropped sharply. Overall, more frequent closed

patterns were discovered for lower minimal-support thresholds, and higher minimal support

thresholds generated fewer closed patterns. Therefore, the trend shown in Figure 3.2 indicates

### 3.8 Chapter Summary

This chapter explored well-established pattern mining techniques combining LDA topic mod-

elling for generic MDS. It proposed a novel approach called PETMSum, which exploits pattern-

enhanced topic models to derive discriminative and semantically rich representations of doc-

ument sets to capture both topics and hidden correlations among text data. Its signiﬁcance

derives from its innovation as the ﬁrst to apply pattern-enhanced topic modelling to solve MDS

problems. Its key feature is its ability to mine patterns at a sentence level instead of focusing on

particular words or documents, thus, enabling it to capture hidden correlations between either

topics and sentences or sentence themselves.

First, a pattern-enhanced topic model was introduced to represent sentences and topics;

this was achieved by establishing pattern-enhanced topic representations for each identiﬁed

topic by discovering topical relevant patterns. This chapter also discussed how and why a

topic selection process is applied in the establishment of the pattern-enhanced intermediate

topic representation for MDS task. Subsequently, a set of novel methods were designed to

measure the importance and information coverage of sentences based on pattern-enhanced

topic representations; this helped discuss the solution to selecting sentences to form generic

summaries, which combined both clustering with an MMR greedy approach and a diversity-

penalty imposition to reduce redundancy. Finally, by conducting extensive experiments on

DUC 2004 summarisation benchmark datasets, this chapter demonstrated the effectiveness of

the proposed approach for generic MDS.

Next chapter will discuss this study’s novel pattern-enhanced solution for another important

task of MDS - query-focused MDS.

## Chapter 4

## Pattern-enhanced Query Relevance Models for

## Query-focused MDS

The Pattern-enhanced Topic Model introduced in Chapter 3 (which derived discriminative and

semantically rich representations of document sets) can capture topic structures and reveal

hidden correlations within text data. However, such topical pattern representations cannot

bias users’ information needs, which are typically speciﬁed by short queries in query-focused

summarisations. Even this study involved topic selection based on a topic’s importance in a

given multi-document set; however, this is not necessarily an appropriate match for a given

query with already identiﬁed important topics. Therefore, in query-focused summarisation, it

is beneﬁcial to establish an effective query relevance model both to represent the relevance of

sentences and to complement a corresponding topic model. In this chapter, a novel pattern-

enhanced query relevance model is introduced and integrated with a pattern-enhanced topic

model in one framework to solve the problem of query-focused MDS.

In special MDS cases, query-focused summarisation deals with both query relevance and

topic coverage in a balanced manner [Luo et al., 2013] to fulﬁl users’ information needs (i.e.,

answering a given query, but also providing additional important information) within a length-

limited text snippet. To address such challenges, it is extremely important to create an accurate

intermediate-representation [Nenkova and McKeown, 2012] for both documents and queries to

capture and measure their key aspects (which are both relevant and important) effectively and

efﬁciently.

However, when considering the topics in a given document set as an implicit query along

63


<!-- Page 91 -->


64 CHAPTER 4. PATTERN-ENHANCED QUERY RELEVANCE MODELS FOR QUERY-FOCUSED MDS

with a given explicit query, creating an intermediate representation introduces a query expansion

problem. From this perspective, and in the context of query-focused MDS, most state-of-the-art

approaches expand key topics and queries in a term-based manner (i.e., to represent topics and

queries as a set of expanded relevant terms). Typically, these methods are effective for query

relevance, as it is generally simple to measure for sentences containing some query relevant

terms. Conversely, for sentences that do not possess any original query terms but otherwise

contain implicit relevant or topically important information, query expansion can become more

complex and challenging, and, sometimes, external or handcrafted resources (such as WordNet,

labelled learning data or web data collection) must be used to generate accurate representations.

Therefore, some novel query expansion techniques are required for a query-focused MDS to

expand both explicit but short query terms and implicit topical terms to produce longer and

more accurate, coherent and discriminative representations of queries and topics.

Therefore, to address the aforementioned problems, this chapter will focus on developing an

effective pattern-based approach for query-focused MDS by combining pattern mining, topic

modelling and query expansion techniques.

### 4.1 Dual Pattern-enhanced Representations for Query-focused MDS

For query-focused summarisations, extracted sentences must not only be relevant to a given

query but also contain the most signiﬁcant information in a set of documents. To meet the

special requirements of query-focused MDS tasks, a dual pattern-enhanced representations

model was proposed to represent explicit query relevance and implicit topical importance to

overcome the limitations of term-based representations. In the proposed model (namely dual

pattern-enhanced representations for query-focused MDS, or DPRQSum), the topic signiﬁcance

of a sentence is represented and measured through topical relevant patterns introduced in

Chapter 3, and the query relevance of sentences is represented by a set of novel query relevant

patterns, which will be proposed in this chapter. Further, to maximise the representative power

of the discovered query relevant patterns, a novel re-weighting algorithm was applied based on

a rough set three-way decision theory. By punishing some unbiased patterns towards user given

queries, a pattern-enhanced query relevance model can represent and measure such relevance in

sentences more accurately.

representations model, DPRQSum measures sentences’ topic signiﬁcance, information cover-

### 4.2 Query Relevance Representations

For relevance modelling, query expansion and pattern mining techniques were incorporated

to generate an intermediate pattern-based query relevance representation for sentences. Using

query expansion to reformulate a seed query is a widely adopted method to improve retrieval

performance in IR operations [Gao et al., 2015]. In the context of query-focused MDS, as a

given query usually consists of very few terms, it is necessary to involve some query expansion

techniques to obtain better query understandings. In the proposed model, query expansion

is combined with pattern mining in an innovative ‘win-win’ manner - that is, applying query

expansion techniques to improve relevant pattern discovery, and exploiting discovered patterns

to improve query expansion.

Step 1: The ﬁrst step attempted to seize more query relevant terms by collecting the co-

occurring terms with original query terms in one sentence. For unsupervised extractive sum-

marisers without any training data or external resources, this method is a reliable choice to help

expand query relevant terms, as it compromises original query terms from a given query and

their co-occurring terms within the same sentence. An example of this is illustrated in Table

### 4.3 Sentence Query Relevance Score

Based on the proposed novel pattern-enhanced query relevance representation, DPRQSum utilises

the signiﬁcance of matched query relevant patterns in a given sentence to measure its relevance

in relation to a query. As query relevant terms are expanded through co-occurring terms with

original query terms in a sentence, the derived pattern-based query relevance representation

may include some uncertain relevant patterns, which consist of co-occurring terms only (i.e.,

without any original query terms). Thus, to minimise such uncertainty, the proposed model

involves a re-weighing process for every query relevant pattern before calculating a sentence’s

query relevance. This borrows from the three-way decision theory [Li et al., 2017, Yao, 2009]

to treat the user information needs (represented by query relevant patterns) as an approximate

concept (a rough set). A pair of lower and upper approximations were then used to divide query

relevant patterns into three disjoint regions: the patterns in the lower approximation, deﬁned as

true-relevant patterns; the patterns in the boundary between upper and lower approximations,

deﬁned as vaguely-relevant patterns; and the patterns in the upper approximation, deﬁned as

false-relevant patterns.

Therefore, both the rough-set theory and three-way decision rules will be introduced (which

are used to re-weight query relevant patterns), including an exploration of how query relevant

This process will help deﬁne how a sentence’s query relevance is measured.

### 4.3.1 Rough Set and Three-way Decision Rules

As a mathematical approach to describe imprecision, vagueness and uncertainty in data analysis,

the rough-set theory was ﬁrst introduced by Pawlak [1982] as a method to deﬁne a formal

approximation of conventional sets - that is, a pair of subsets deﬁning both the lower and upper

approximations of an original set [Pawlak et al., 1988, Pawlak, 1997]. If a concept cannot

be characterised by the relatively certain information regarding its elements, a rough set can

use this pair of precise concepts (i.e., the lower and upper approximations) to approximately

describe such vague concepts. Li et al. [2000, 2017] attempted to use a rough set model to

deﬁne users’ information needs and succeeded in their applications of IF and text classiﬁcation.

The pair of the lower and the upper approximations divide the approximation space of

objects into three distinct regions: the positive region, the boundary region, and the negative

region.

Given that a universe U contains a ﬁnite set of objects (e.g. patterns), the lower approxima-

tion and the upper approximation are denoted as A (X) and ¯A (X) respectively for the arbitrary

subset X ⊑U; thus, the positive region POS (X), the boundary region BND (X), and the

negative region NEG (X) are deﬁned as:

POS (X) = A (X)

BND (X) = ¯A (X) −A (X)

NEG (X) = U −¯A (X)

### 4.4 Overall Sentence Ranking Based on Balanced Topic Coverage and

## Query Relevance in Query-focused MDS

In a query-focused summarisation, overall sentence ranking is determined by a combination of

two factors [Nenkova and McKeown, 2012]: query relevance measuring a sentence’s relevance

in relation to a given query and the topic coverage or importance measuring its importance

within a collection of documents. In a DPRQSum model, the topic coverage and importance of

sentences are estimated based on topical relevant patterns and query relevance is derived from

query relevant patterns.

Importantly, the topic coverage of sentences here differs from the topic coverage require-

ment for query-focused MDS, as the latter functions at a summary-document level, which

requires generated summaries to reserve important topics as much as possible for a given

document set, while the former indicates a sentence’s level of information coverage, regardless

of how many topics it covers. Further, if a sentence presents only one important topic within

an entire document set, it is still considered a good candidate to form a summary. Therefore,

the topical signiﬁcance of a sentence is deﬁned as an evaluation metric that indicates both a

sentence’s level of important information - so called topic coverage - and its distinctiveness - so

called topic novelty - when ranking query-focused MDS. The latter is a more important factor

in query-focused MDS tasks than in generic MDS, as the score measuring a sentence’s topical

### 4.5 Greedy Sentence Selection with Redundancy Reduction

For MDS tasks with maximal information coverage and relevance reserved, redundancy re-

moval becomes a fated process during the sentence selection stage. Similar to the PETMSum

proposed in Chapter 3, the proposed DPRQSum also adopts a greedy MMR approach [Car-

bonell and Goldstein, 1998] with a diversity penalty imposition [Wan, 2008, Yan and Wan,

2014] applied for sentence selection. However, unlike PETMSum (in which a diversity-penalty

is applied inside each topic cluster), DPRQsum applies the imposition over one top-n ranking

sentence pool. As such, the ﬁrst sentence in the ﬁnal summary had the highest ranking score

in this pool and sentences with the highest diversity-penalty-imposed score in the remaining

sentences were then individually added, using Equation 3.6, as formulated in SRRank [Yan and

Wan, 2014].

The penalty weight parameter δ here can be empirically tuned for the best result. Both

the selection and penalisation were completed in an iterative manner until the summary length

reached the limit [Wu et al., 2016].

The algorithm 5 describes the process of summary sentence selection with redundancy

reduction applied.

### 4.6 Experiments and Evaluation

In this section, three sets of experiments were conducted to verify three hypotheses:

• Hypothesis 1: The proposed pattern-enhanced models (including both PETMSum-Q and

DPRQSum) are effective for query-focused MDS, as compared to other state-of-the-art

unsupervised extractive summarisation systems.

• Hypothesis 2: The model having dual pattern-based representations for topic importance

and query relevance performs better than a singleton pattern-based representation model

for query-focused MDS tasks.

• Hypothesis 3: Exploiting an innovative re-weighting process for query relevant patterns

can represent sentences’ query relevance more accurately than using query relevant pat-

terns alone.

Along with the DPRQSum, the evaluation of PETMSum-Q (the Pattern-enhanced Topic

Model for Query-focused MDS) that we introduced in last chapter also has been done and

presented in this section.

### 4.6.1 Dataset

The proposed methods were evaluated on two datasets of DUC 2006 and DUC 2007, both of

which are open benchmarks dataset from DUC for automatic summarisation evaluation. Query-

focused MDS constitutes the main task focus of DUC 2006 and DUC 2007, and helped model

real-world complex question answering - that is, a question cannot be answered by simply

stating information pertaining a name, date or quantity. DUC 2006 and DUC 2007 consisted

of 50 and 45 topics, respectively, and each topic included a topic description and a document

set with ﬁxed number of 25 news articles. The task was to create a summary of no more than

250 words for each document set to answer particular question(s) in a topic statement. Both

DUC 2006 and DUC 2007 provided at least four human-written reference summaries of each

document collection for evaluation. The datasets are brieﬂy described in Table 4.4.

### 4.6.2 Evaluation Metrics

The ROUGE toolkit [Lin, 2004] was used to evaluate the performance of this study’s proposed

summarisation systems. In this experiment, the ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-SU4 scores

were reported 2 with their corresponding 95% conﬁdential intervals. ROUGE-1 based on

unigram evaluates how well a testing summary was consistent with human judgements [Lin

and Hovy, 2003], the ROUGE-2 measures the overlap of bigrams and ROUGE-SU4 examines

the overlap of skip-bigrams with a maximum skip distance of four. Skip-bigrams measures

the overlap of any pair words in their sentence order allowing arbitrary gaps between them.

Generally, the higher the ROUGE scores, the more similar they are to creating ‘ideal’ (or

superior) summaries.

### 4.6.3 Baselines

To evaluate the overall performance of the proposed PETMSum-Q and DPRQSum models,

each was compared to a variety of baseline methods, including National Institute of Standards

and Technology (NIST) baselines, two hierarchical topic model based summarisers and several

state-of-the-art unsupervised extractive query-focused summarisation systems.

• NIST baseline - Lead [Wasson, 1998]: is an unsupervised extraction-based summari-

sation approach, which takes the leading sentences one by one (up to 250 words) from

the chronologically ordered documents in a given document set; it is a standard baseline

provided by NIST in both DUC 2006 and DUC 2007.

### 4.8.1 Weight Coefﬁcient of Query Relevance Model

## Chapter 5

## Pattern-enhanced Uncertainty Reduction Model

## for Users’ Information Needs

Evidently, information overload is becoming an increasingly challenging issue. However, au-

tomatic MDS is an important research process that can address this modern problem. Other

important endeavours regard IF and IR. Just like MDS (including both generic and query-

focused MDS), the most basic requirement of these systems is to satisfy users’ information

needs. However, what is a factual account of users’ information needs? Sometimes, even

users themselves cannot describe their own desires clearly and accurately. The additional

(and often unavoidable) uncertainties of natural language text (such as polysemy, synonymy,

semantic uncertainty and discourse-level uncertainty) can further impede one’s expressions.

This ambiguity constitutes a major part of the gap between such needs and the corresponding

information resources that are available. Most IR and IF models attempt to ﬁll this gap by

applying some effective relevance matching methods to the given input information. However,

since uncertainty is generally caused by a lack of information [Zimmermann, 2000], query

expansion techniques are a common solution to aid short user queries or simple user proﬁles.

Some IR and IF models use supervised learning from labelled training data to model users’

information needs [Gao et al., 2015, Li et al., 2017]), while other unsupervised learning models

employ external resources [Xu et al., 2009] or Pseudo-relevance feedback [Andrzejewski and

Buttler, 2011, Miao et al., 2016] to expand queries and improve certainty. However, labelled

training data and external resources are not always available or feasible, and neither are reliable

enough, particularly as human-made assessments generally bear varying degrees of ambiguity

themselves. Thus, is there any alternative approach to reduce the uncertainty of these global

93


<!-- Page 121 -->

information needs?

It is typical practice to ﬁlter out irrelevant or unimportant data before applying summari-

sation that uses some IR or IF techniques. However, this area has not been explored in great

depth. Unlike most IR or IF systems that treat text data in a document space, MDS systems

analyse text data at a sentence level. Assumedly, more detailed sentence spaces possess less

uncertain information than document spaces, and such sentence-level analysis should improve

the certainty of models gauging users’ information needs. As investigated, pattern-enhanced

models can beneﬁt summarisation, thus, proving the proposed pattern-enhanced sentence rank-

ing model’s ability to not only discover important and relevant sentences, but also detect noisy

information from input text data - each of which are irrelevant to users’ information needs.

However, can this ‘side effect’ beneﬁt IR or IF by eliminating bottom ranked sentences from

input documents and, in turn, eventually reduce this unwanted uncertainty? Therefore, this

chapter will investigate how a pattern-enhanced sentence level ranking model can be used to

reduce the uncertainty or ‘fuzziness’ of users’ information needs.

### 5.1 Pattern-enhanced Uncertainty Reduction Model

As introduced in Chapter 4, users’ information needs consist of implicit topic interests and

explicit queries. Therefore, a dual pattern-enhanced model was introduced to represent each for

query-focused MDS. Topical relevant patterns discovered by the pattern-enhanced topic model

proposed in Chapter 3 can be used to represent the implicit topic interests of users, and the query

relevance model proposed in Chapter 4 can represent their explicit query-relevant interests.

Thus, the users’ information needs now can be represented by topical relevant patterns and

query relevant patterns.

Based on this dual pattern-enhanced representations model, a sentence ranking model using

Equation 4.7 to ﬁlter out bottom-ranked sentences and reduce uncertainty in users’ information

need was created. Figure 5.1 illustrates the process of the proposed pattern-enhanced sentence-

ranking model for this uncertainty reduction.

First, the proposed model transferred input data from document space to sentence space (i.e.,

transferring multiple documents to one single set of sentences); next, it applied both a pattern-

enhanced topic model and a pattern-enhanced relevance model to discover topically relevant

and query relevant patterns from this space to represent users’ needs. Based on these pattern-

enhanced representations, it scored and ranked every sentence to detect noisy information at

a sentence level. Subsequently, the model ﬁltered out the bottom-ranked sentences, retaining

only the top ranks to comprise new uncertainty reduced sentence space (i.e., a subset of original

input sentences). Finally, this pre-ﬁltered input was used to feed the IR, IF and MDS models

to achieve a better performance for uncertainty reduced user information needs. For supervised

iterations of these models, this reduction process can be applied to learning models with labelled

training data to reduce uncertainty in training data. However, without such data, this process

can be exploited to generate pseudo-feedback or pseudo-training data by extracting top-ranked

sentences to improve performance.

In summary, the proposed pattern-enhanced sentence ranking model can reduce the uncer-

tainty of users’ information needs by applying the following strategies:

• Using sentence space rather than document or term space can help represent users’ in-

formation needs more accurately, as sentences contain more speciﬁc and discriminate

meanings, as well as more complete and correlate information.

• Topic selection in pattern-enhanced topic models identiﬁes certain topics and discards

uncertain topics (see Section 3.2 and 3.7.3).

• Building a pair of pattern sets, query relevant patterns and background patterns, to

comprise pattern-enhanced relevance representations (see Section 4.2) and applying novel

(see Section 4.2) can both reduce the uncertainty of query relevant patterns expanded

from users’ queries.

• Filtering out noisy or irrelevant information from users’ information needs by eliminating

bottom-ranked sentences from input documents can help reduce the uncertainty of input

data.

### 5.1.1 Building the Sentence Space

Classic IR and IF models consider the input document corpus as a document space in which

each individual document is treated as a separate point. Different coordinate systems based

on different representative features (or the numerical weights of representative features) can be

built to describe and locate a document in this space, thus, ensuring that a continuous degree of

similarity between queries and documents can be calculated and that documents can be ranked

according to their possible relevance. Therefore, within this space, users’ information needs can

be deﬁned by a set of relevant documents. Conversely, as a document is typically comprised of

various information factors, it offers more uncertainty than a sentence.

*Figure 5.2 provides a graphic view of users’ information needs over a space of documents*

whereas the grid formed with smaller cells is the sentence space, with the circle indicating

users’ information needs. While the circle line passes through, the shaded document grids

represent documents’ elementary sets of information needs, and the shaded sentence cells

indicate sentences’ elementary sets; in some of these document grids or sentence cells, there

are some surrounding parts that are outside the circle line, indicating the general uncertainty of

information needs. Thus, from this example, it is clear that uncertainty in a document space is

much larger than that in a sentence space.

Moreover, as long documents are poorly represented due to their reduced similarity values

derived from a small scalar product and large dimensionality, measuring the relevance between

long documents and short queries is more inefﬁcient and ineffective than measuring the rele-

vance between a sentence and a given query. Thus, the proposed uncertainty reduction model

transforms a set of documents input to a set of sentences for which the topically and query

relevant representations of users’ information needs are both established over a sentence space.

### 5.1.2 Discarding the Uncertain Topics

In the proposed uncertainty reduction model, two different but complementary pattern sets were

used to represent users’ information needs: topical relevant patterns and query relevant patterns.

The uncertainty in users’ implicit topic interests can be caused by the topical uncertainty of a

given document collection or by users’ ambiguous descriptions (i.e., a given query). As there are

two representations, the task to reduce uncertainty caused by users’ queries was transferred to

the process of generating query relevant pattern representations. Also, a topic selection strategy

that discovered topical relevant patterns was integrated to reduce the topical uncertainty in a

given document collection.

The topical uncertainty in this input data consisted of two major factors: the uncertain topic

number and uncertain topic importance. Different document collections may have a different

number of topics involved, and different topics in one collection may have a different level of

importance - that is, some may be very important, while others may not. An LDA topic model

was also applied to identify the topic structure of the given documents; however, the number

of topics had to be selected manually - indeed, determining the optimal number of topics to

achieve equally optimal results is difﬁcult. Therefore, although one can order LDAs to ﬁnd

as many or as few topics, they must still identify the amount of found topics that are more

important to users’ information needs. As this number should be lower than the discovered


<!-- Page 125 -->


98 CHAPTER 5. PATTERN-ENHANCED UNCERTAINTY REDUCTION MODEL FOR USERS’ INFORMATION NEEDS

topics in one document collection, selecting a subset of found topics can help reduce topical

uncertainty. Further, the focused topics (i.e., topics appearing often and with high distribution

in a collection) should be more important to users than sparse topics with small distribution.

In Section 3.2, a topic selection strategy with two constraint thresholds of maximal covered

topic number (nt) and minimal topic weight (wt) was introduced to deﬁne the number of

dynamically selected topics according to the discovered topic structure. Let T be the topic

set in a document collection D (as discovered by LDA topic modeling), with two thresholds nt

(0 < nt < |T|) and wt. Thus, the uncertain topics deﬁned as follows:

Deﬁnition 5. (uncertain topics): a topic Z in T is called an uncertain topic if its topic weight

W(Z) < wt (a given threshold of minimal topic weight), or, its ranking number of topic weight

R(Z) > nt (a given threshold of maximal covered topic number).

The uncertain topics are considered as irrelevant topics with too much uncertain information

to represent users’ topical interests. In the proposed uncertainty reduction model, the topic

selection process decreased the uncertainty level of given input topic structures by discarding

some ‘certain’ unimportant (or uncertain) topics. By applying this selection strategy, the topical

uncertainty in the input document collection can be reduced, as compared to using all the topics

found by an LDA.

It is worth noting that the main purpose of this topic selection in the proposed uncertainty

reduction model is to reduce the topical uncertainty caused by uncertain topic structures in

input documents; it is not used to identify certain relevant topics for users’ information needs,

as neither user given queries nor proﬁles are involved. However, if using other topic weight

systems that do involve such features to measure topical relevance in relation to users’ needs,

this topic selection strategy can be applied.

### 5.1.3 Re-weighting Uncertain Relevant Patterns

To reduce the inﬂuence of uncertainty, a sentence space rather than a document space was

established over the input document corpus. In this, each sentence was represented through a

vector containing the representative patterns’ weights, which constituted either topical patterns

or query relevant patterns representing users’ information needs. However, these representative

patterns possessed different descriptiveness power. For example, the query relevant pattern


<!-- Page 126 -->


5.1. PATTERN-ENHANCED UNCERTAINTY REDUCTION MODEL 99

‘school music’ that occurred in 20 sentences may be more powerful than the pattern ‘school

principle’, which occurred in only 3 sentences. To make those patterns more accurate for

representing users’ information needs, the input sentence space was separated to two parts:

one for the query-relevant sentence space for sentences containing at least one original query

term and another for the background sentence space containing sentences without any original

query terms. Assumedly, the uncertainty in query-relevant sentence spaces is signiﬁcantly

less than the latter. However, one cannot consider that sentences in background spaces are

wholly irrelevant to users’ information needs. For example, if a query relevant pattern exists

in 10 sentences of both a query-relevant and background sentence space, is its descriptiveness

power the same as another pattern that exists in 10 sentences in the former but not the latter?

Indeed, they should not be treated equally when ranking sentence’s relevance. Therefore,

based on the rough set three-way decision theory, the background sentence space was used

as a shadow reference to re-weight the descriptiveness power of query relevant patterns (see

Section 4.3) and calculate the relevancy between sentences and users’ information needs more

accurately. By applying this process with two separated sentence spaces, the relations between

the relevant sentence space and background space can be discovered and examined. Indeed,

such relations may reveal the cognitive framework of users’ needs (i.e., the true relations

between such requests and other identiﬁed representative features, such as query terms, co-

occurring words (patterns), topic distribution and contextual information).

As introduced in previous chapters, a paired set of query-relevant patterns XQ and back-

ground patterns XB can be derived for a given input documents set D from query-relevant

sentence set SQ and background sentence set SB. Thus, the following deﬁnition for uncertain

relevant patterns can be introduced:

Deﬁnition 6. (uncertain relevant patterns): If a pattern x ∈XQ and x ∈XB too, pattern x

is an uncertain relevant pattern.

Based on this deﬁnition, some properties regarding uncertain relevant patterns can be de-

rived as follows:

Property 1: the uncertain relevant patterns do not contain any original query terms.

Property 2: given that the corresponding support of an uncertain relevant pattern in XQ is

less than its corresponding support in XB (such that suppQ(x) < suppB(x)), the uncertainty

level of x is greater than an uncertain relevant pattern x′, of which suppQ(x′) > suppB(x′) (i.e.

### 5.2 Experimental Design

This section addresses a set of experiments conducted to verify two hypotheses:

• Hypothesis 1: the proposed pattern-enhanced sentence ranking model can reduce the

uncertainty of users’ information needs for IR, IF and MDS models.

• Hypothesis 2: the uncertainty-reduced input data can improve the performance of IR, IF

and MDS models.

### 5.2.1 Dataset and Evaluation Metrics

Experiments to verify these two hypotheses were conducted on two datasets, DUC 2006 and

DUC 2007 (see detailed dataset description in Section 4.6.1), which are both open-benchmark

datasets designed to evaluate query-focused MDS systems. Considering a query-focused MDS

dataset should contain more ‘noisy’ information compared to generic MDS datasets, this se-

lection is used to evaluate the proposed uncertainty reduction model. As revealed, ROUGE

evaluation metrics (ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-SU4) were investigated during the

experiment and their average recall values were then reported.


<!-- Page 130 -->


5.2. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN 103

### 5.2.2 Implemented Methods

The proposed uncertainty reduction model was applied to generate downsized input for some

widely used generic summarisers (designed to generate summaries without focusing on user

speciﬁed queries) and transform them into query-focused summarisers, which also generate

summaries according to speciﬁc needs. By comparing the performance of original summarisers

and transformed summarisers undertaking the same query-focused MDS task on the same

dataset, the two tested hypotheses can be veriﬁed.

The following widely used generic summarisers were implemented and transformed for

evaluation:

• LSA [Gong and Liu, 2001]: is a method using latent semantic analysis on terms to

extracts semantically important sentences with the greatest combined weights across all

important topics.

• SumFocus [Vanderwende et al., 2007]: is a variety version of SumBasic [Nenkova and

Vanderwende, 2005] that produces summaries by extracting words with high document

frequency and high topic probabilities.

• KLSum [Haghighi and Vanderwende, 2009]: is an unsupervised method that greedily

adds sentences to a summary, given it decreases the KL Divergence.

• TextRank [Mihalcea and Tarau, 2004]: is an unsupervised graph method for MDS that

extracts keywords and sentences using co-occurring relations and overlap-based similar-

ity relations.

• LexRank [Erkan and Radev, 2004b]: is a graph method that selects the most signiﬁcant

sentences by calculating their lexical eigenvector centrality in a sentence connectivity

graph, which is constructed based on sentence-to-sentence cosine similarity.

These implemented models were based on a Python open-source library Sumy 2, which

extracts summaries from single documents. For this experiment, Sumy had been specially

modiﬁed to perform MDS task.

### 5.3 Experimental Results

### 5.3.1 Overall Performance Comparisons

Experiments to verify the effectiveness of the proposed pattern-enhanced uncertainty reduction

model for query-focused MDS tasks were conducted. Two parameters of reduction rate η and

weight coefﬁcient ϱ using a gradient method were tuned for evaluation. Rate η was varied from

95% to 10% with a 5% decrease each time. For ϱ, since the effects of this parameter for query-

focused MDS evaluation were already presented in Section 4.8), its three most representative

values were selected to combine with η in this experiment. On the DUC 2006 dataset, ϱ =

1, 0.9, 0.8, and on DUC 2007 dataset, ϱ = 1, 0.8, 0.5; these ﬁgures were selected according

to this coefﬁcient’s individual effects on the two datasets. The overall performance results are

presented in Tables 5.2 and 5.3; however, not every test result from the different combinations of

these two parameters are reported, as only representative combinations are shown (i.e., the best

performance and some illustrating a trend towards the best results). For every testing model,

the original ROUGE scores are also listed, namely Before along with the best results (denoted

as After - best), which were generated by the transformed model upon applying the proposed

uncertainty reduction method with different parameter settings. The overall best results and the

greatest individual improvements for each testing model are represented in bold.

Evidently, almost every transformation with different reduction rates improved the perfor-

mance of the implemented model for all three ROUGE metrics. In one group of experiments on

each model, at least one transformed model improved signiﬁcantly (greater than 5% in terms of

the most representative ROUGE score of ROUGE-2. Additionally, the best scores became more

comparable to the bestSys scores than their original performance. Such results demonstrate that

the proposed uncertainty reduction model is both an effective and feasible method to improve

different MDS models’ performance when reducing uncertainty in users’ information needs.

As shown in both Tables 5.3 and 5.2, , the TextRank and LexRank improvements (two

notably strong performers) peaked at approximately half reduction (45% reduction rate) on the

5.4. DISCUSSION 107

### 5.4 Discussion

As indicated by this study’s results, leveraging pattern-enhanced sentence ranking models for

uncertainty reduction can greatly improve the performance of an MDS model to meet users’

information needs more effectively and accurately. Evidently, applying a sentence-level ranking

method to input document sets to ﬁlter out unnecessary information generated results with

consequentially less uncertainty, which, thus, better matched users’ queries. Most importantly,

these information needs were also represented and measured more accurately through a com-

bination of topical patterns and query-relevant patterns, which provided concrete and precise

semantic meanings to both users’ implicit topic interest and explicit query relevant needs.

Further, applying more focused analyses on sentence space rather than document space enabled

for greater detection of queries’ uncertainty and fuzziness, which, in turn, could be reduced

more effectively and efﬁciently.

The evaluation results also demonstrate the potential effectiveness of the proposed uncer-

tainty reduction model in both supervised and unsupervised user model learning. The former

model trains input labelled data, which are supposed to contain certain information for identify-

ing users’ true information needs, but instead contain different levels of uncertainty. Applying

the proposed method to decrease uncertainty in input labelled data can deﬁnitely improve the

certainty of such user models. If the labelled data are too few to generate an accurate model

of users’ information needs, applying the uncertainty reduction model to unlabelled data to

generate more ‘pseudo’ labelled data (which highly matched either labelled data or users’ needs)

can improve the accuracy of semi-supervised or unsupervised learning methods.

Since the experiments and evaluation were only completed with MDS systems on MDS

datasets, query-focused MDS tasks can be considered as somewhat similar to IF or IR tasks, as

each must satisfy users’ information needs. Thus, the effectiveness of the proposed uncertainty

reduction model requires further evaluation with IF and IR systems and datasets.

Though convincing results that verify the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed model

have been produced, it still contains some limitations:

• Using query terms and co-occurring terms to separate sentence space may generate some

uncertainty, as not all co-occurrences indicate relevance, and sentences without query

terms are not always irrelevant to users’ needs. Thus, more advanced techniques must


<!-- Page 135 -->


108 CHAPTER 5. PATTERN-ENHANCED UNCERTAINTY REDUCTION MODEL FOR USERS’ INFORMATION NEEDS

be sought to expand query terms to construct relevant and irrelevant sentence spaces to

derive pattern-enhanced representations of users’ information needs more precisely.

• Using statistical topic distribution to identify uncertain topics may miss some query rele-

vant topics with very small distribution, but which may still be relevant to users’ queries.

Thus, obtaining query terms and user proﬁles should be considered when identifying

relevant topics.

• Algorithm for re-weighting uncertain relevant patterns may need further optimisation on

parameters tuning and odds function formulation.

• It is difﬁcult to determine an optimal reduction rate for input reduction, thus, potentially

limiting the practicality of the proposed uncertainty reduction model.

### 5.5 Chapter Summary

This chapter proposed an uncertainty reduction model using a novel pattern-enhanced sentence

ranking method to reduce input uncertainty and achieve better matched results with users’

information needs. This sentence ranking method was theoretically explored through a detailed

analysis within the context of reducing uncertainty during users’ information needs extraction.

Extensive experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposed model using DUC 2006 and

DUC 2007 data collections to transform generic summarisers to query-focused summarisers,

which produce signiﬁcantly better summaries that satisfy users’ needs.

Based on these results, the proposed model’s performance and its effects on key parameters

were analysed, along with a brief discussion on its novelty, effectiveness and its limitations.
